subtopic_detail: selecting which medicine to withdraw first in a frail older woman with recurrent falls and postural hypotension
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 84 year old woman who has fallen three times in two months, most recently sustaining a skin tear to her forearm. She lives alone with daily assistance from her daughter.

She describes light headedness on standing from a chair and says the falls all happened shortly after she got up. Her medicines are perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night taken intermittently, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily and doxazosin 4 mg daily, which was started three months ago for nocturia. Her blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with reproduction of her symptoms. Her cognition is intact, her gait is steady when she is not light headed, her vitamin D is replete and her vision was checked this year.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with symptoms reproduced, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 14 seconds, no focal neurological deficit, no cerebellar signs, no peripheral neuropathy, heart sounds dual with no murmur, skin tear dressed on the left forearm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 76 nmol/L (50-150), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality, morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: Which medication would you withdraw first?

options.text: Atorvastatin, since its benefit at her age is limited and it may cause myalgia
options.rationale: Statins are frequently reviewed in frail older people and may reasonably be stopped where life expectancy is short or the indication is primary prevention. They do not cause orthostatic hypotension, so withdrawing the statin would not address the mechanism producing her falls. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Pantoprazole, since long term use is associated with fracture and infection risk
options.rationale: Long term proton pump inhibitor use without a continuing indication is a legitimate deprescribing target, associated with hip fracture, hypomagnesaemia and enteric infection. It is not a cause of postural blood pressure drop and is therefore not the first priority in a patient falling because of orthostatic symptoms. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Amlodipine, since calcium channel blockade causes vasodilatation and ankle oedema
options.rationale: Amlodipine contributes to her overall blood pressure lowering and is a reasonable later target as her regimen is simplified. Dihydropyridines cause considerably less orthostatic hypotension than alpha blockade because they do not impair the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains pressure on standing. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Doxazosin, since alpha blockade directly impairs the vasoconstrictor reflex on standing
options.rationale: Alpha one blockade prevents the peripheral vasoconstriction that normally maintains blood pressure on standing, making it the drug most specifically responsible for a symptomatic 36 mmHg systolic drop, and the temporal link to its introduction three months ago matches the onset of her falls. It also has the weakest indication in the list, having been started for nocturia in a woman for whom safer alternatives exist. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Temazepam, since benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls in older adults
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is an important goal in anyone over 65 who is falling and this drug should certainly come out in due course. It is taken only intermittently and at night, whereas her falls occur on standing during the day with a reproducible postural drop, which points to a different mechanism. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

explanation.summary: Deprescribing in frail older people works best when it is mechanism driven rather than list driven, starting with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm. This woman has symptomatic orthostatic hypotension with a 36 mmHg systolic drop that reproduces her symptoms, and her falls all occur on standing. Alpha one blockers such as doxazosin and prazosin directly prevent the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains blood pressure on standing, which makes them the most potent orthostatic offenders among common antihypertensives. The temporal association with its introduction three months ago and the weakness of its indication strengthen the case further. Several of her other medicines are legitimate deprescribing targets and should be addressed sequentially afterwards, changing one drug at a time so that the effect of each withdrawal can be judged.
key_points: Alpha one blockers impair reflex vasoconstriction and are potent causes of orthostatic hypotension.
A symptomatic postural drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic defines orthostatic hypotension.
Deprescribing should start with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm.
Temporal association between starting a drug and the onset of symptoms is strong supporting evidence.
Withdraw one drug at a time so that the effect of each change can be attributed.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure before choosing which medicine to stop in a falling older patient, and start with the alpha blocker when there is a symptomatic postural drop, because alpha one blockade abolishes the reflex vasoconstriction that other antihypertensives leave intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

subtopic_detail: choosing therapy for amiodarone associated thyrotoxicosis when the gland shows absent vascularity
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar asked to see a 68 year old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for fourteen months for recurrent ventricular tachycardia after an infarct. His implanted defibrillator has fired twice in the past fortnight.

Over three months he has lost 9 kg despite a good appetite, and he has a fine tremor and heat intolerance. He grew up in Adelaide and has no history of iodine deficiency or previous thyroid disease. There is no neck swelling and no eye signs. His thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine. His thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies are both negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows a normal sized gland with absent parenchymal vascularity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min irregular, blood pressure 138/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine resting tremor, warm moist palms, no goitre or thyroid bruit, no proptosis or lid retraction, no pretibial change, defibrillator generator palpable below the left clavicle
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 11.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies negative, colour flow Doppler shows absent parenchymal vascularity, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: High dose carbimazole alone titrated against repeat thyroid function testing
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are the treatment where excess iodine drives an overactive gland, typically in a patient with a pre-existing nodular goitre or latent Graves disease and preserved or increased Doppler flow. They cannot help where the gland is not synthesising hormone at all but is releasing preformed stores as it is destroyed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral corticosteroid for destructive thyroiditis with cardiology review of the amiodarone
options.rationale: Absent parenchymal vascularity with negative antibodies, no goitre and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate in an iodine replete patient indicates a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone, which responds to corticosteroid rather than to synthesis blockade. Whether to stop amiodarone is a separate cardiological judgement rather than an automatic step, because its half life of around one hundred days means cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit while withdrawal risks recurrence of the ventricular tachycardia his defibrillator is already treating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease amiodarone and observe, since the thyrotoxicosis will settle once it clears
options.rationale: Stopping the drug is often appropriate in principle and achieves nothing quickly, because amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life measured in months, so tissue iodine loading persists long after the last dose. Observation also leaves a thyrotoxic state that is actively destabilising his ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid arranged as an outpatient procedure
options.rationale: Radioiodine requires the gland to take up iodine, and the enormous iodine load delivered by amiodarone saturates the sodium iodide symporter and suppresses radioiodine uptake to negligible levels for many months. The treatment is therefore ineffective in this setting regardless of which subtype is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Potassium perchlorate with lithium carbonate to block further iodide uptake
options.rationale: Perchlorate competitively inhibits iodide transport into the thyroid and is used as an adjunct in the iodine induced subtype or in mixed disease unresponsive to first line therapy, often alongside a thionamide. Blocking uptake is illogical in a destructive process where stored hormone is leaking from a gland that is not trapping iodide. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is highly lipophilic, and it causes thyrotoxicosis by two mechanisms that require opposite treatments. Type 1 is iodine induced excess synthesis in a gland with pre-existing pathology such as a nodular goitre or latent Graves disease, and it shows normal or increased vascularity on colour flow Doppler with often positive antibodies, responding to thionamides with or without perchlorate. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis in which preformed hormone leaks from a damaged gland, showing absent vascularity, negative antibodies, no goitre and often a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and it responds to corticosteroid. Mixed forms occur and are treated with both. Radioiodine is ineffective because the iodine load suppresses uptake, and stopping amiodarone produces no rapid benefit given a half life of around one hundred days, so the decision to continue it rests on the cardiac indication.
key_points: Type 1 is iodine induced hormone synthesis in an abnormal gland with preserved or increased Doppler vascularity.
Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis with absent vascularity, negative antibodies and no goitre.
Thionamides treat type 1 and corticosteroid treats type 2, with both used in mixed disease.
Radioiodine is ineffective because the amiodarone iodine load suppresses thyroidal uptake for months.
Amiodarone has a half life of about one hundred days, so cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit.
explanation.pearls: Use colour flow Doppler to separate the two forms of amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis before prescribing, because absent parenchymal vascularity means a destructive thyroiditis that needs corticosteroid rather than carbimazole, and stopping the amiodarone changes nothing for months while risking the arrhythmia it was prescribed for.

subtopic_detail: sequencing thiamine and glucose in a high anion gap acidosis where the blood sugar is not raised
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 49 year old man brought in by ambulance with two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He drinks a bottle of spirits most days and has eaten almost nothing for three days since his last drink.

He is alert and oriented but looks unwell and dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. He has no focal abdominal tenderness, no guarding and no organomegaly. He has no history of diabetes and takes no medication. He has not taken any paracetamol, aspirin, antifreeze or methylated spirits, and his partner confirms there were no tablets or unusual containers at home. His venous gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap, his blood glucose is 4.1 mmol/L, his serum ketones are strongly positive, his lactate is mildly raised and his osmolar gap is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 114/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor, alert and oriented with Glasgow coma scale 15, no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, gait not tested, abdomen soft with generalised mild tenderness, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.24 with bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32) and anion gap 24 mmol/L, blood glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta hydroxybutyrate strongly positive, lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), osmolar gap normal, ethanol not detected, paracetamol and salicylate not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence an intravenous insulin infusion with hourly blood glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Insulin is the treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis, where hyperglycaemia drives the osmotic diuresis and insulin deficiency drives the ketogenesis. This man has a normal blood glucose and is not insulin deficient, so an insulin infusion would cause profound hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis directly
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidaemia below a pH of about 7.1 with haemodynamic compromise, and it does not address the underlying ketogenesis. In this condition the acidosis resolves rapidly once substrate and volume are restored, so bicarbonate would risk rebound alkalosis and hypokalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start fomepizole and arrange urgent haemodialysis for presumed toxic alcohol ingestion
options.rationale: Toxic alcohol poisoning produces a high anion gap acidosis and must always be considered, and it characteristically raises the osmolar gap and is not accompanied by strongly positive ketones. His osmolar gap is normal and there is no history of ingestion, which together make this very unlikely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral carbohydrate and observe him for symptomatic improvement overnight
options.rationale: Restoring carbohydrate is the right principle and the oral route is unreliable in a man who has been vomiting for two days and is clinically dehydrated. He needs intravenous volume and substrate, and observation alone would leave both the ketosis and the volume deficit uncorrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intravenous thiamine followed by glucose containing fluid with volume replacement
options.rationale: Starvation and alcohol deplete glycogen and raise the ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, driving ketogenesis with a normal glucose, so the treatment is carbohydrate and volume rather than insulin. Thiamine must be given before the glucose because it is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and a glucose load in a depleted patient consumes the remaining stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis develops when a person with alcohol dependence stops eating and drinking, typically because of vomiting, and presents with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, strongly positive ketones and a blood glucose that is normal or even low. The mechanism is glycogen depletion combined with a raised ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide from ethanol metabolism, which suppresses gluconeogenesis and shifts the redox state towards beta hydroxybutyrate. Because beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, urine ketone dipsticks that detect acetoacetate may substantially understate the ketosis. Treatment is intravenous glucose and saline, which suppresses ketogenesis by restoring substrate and stimulating insulin, together with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement. Thiamine must precede the glucose, and toxic alcohol ingestion should be excluded by checking the osmolar gap.
key_points: A high anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal or low glucose distinguishes this from diabetic ketoacidosis.
Glycogen depletion and a raised reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide ratio drive the ketogenesis.
Beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, so acetoacetate based urine dipsticks understate the ketosis.
Treatment is glucose and saline rather than insulin, with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement.
A normal osmolar gap argues against toxic alcohol ingestion as the cause of the acidosis.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in a patient with alcohol dependence, because glucose consumes the last of the thiamine as a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in someone who arrived neurologically intact.
